title: Oil Hits Six-Week High as Brent Tops $95 on Twin Strait Supply Fears
excerpt: Brent crude settled up 3.36% at $94.07 after briefly touching $95.47, as the US-Iran conflict escalated and Houthis announced a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia.
body:
Oil prices surged to their highest settlement in six weeks on Wednesday, with Brent crude briefly piercing $95 a barrel before settling at $94.07, as an escalating US-Iran conflict and a Houthi threat to blockade Saudi Arabia revived fears of prolonged supply disruptions across two critical shipping chokepoints.

Brent futures rose $3.06, or 3.36%, marking a fourth consecutive session of gains and the largest four-day dollar increase since April 29, according to FactSet. US West Texas Intermediate crude climbed $2.49, or 2.95%, to $86.83 — also a six-week high.

Twin Strait Crisis Reshapes Supply Calculus

The energy market now faces what traders are calling a "dual-strait worry." The Strait of Hormuz, which carried roughly a fifth of the world's oil supply before the war began, has seen daily crossings effectively stall since the ceasefire collapsed. Iran's Revolutionary Guards' spokesperson escalated further on Wednesday, warning shipping companies on X that the strait's southern route is mined.

President Trump responded with his most explicit threat yet, posting on Truth Social that the United States would "bomb and destroy ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT, including those located next to, or in, the Capital City of Tehran" each time Iran targets a ship in the strait.

"If we continue to see this kind of escalation then we're going to see a very big hike because we're going to be developing into a much wider and much deeper war."

— Joe DeLaura, Senior Energy Strategist, Rabobank

Simultaneously, Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis opened a second front by announcing a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia and threatening to target vessels carrying Saudi oil through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the Red Sea's southern entrance. Five tankers in the Red Sea diverted on Wednesday to avoid the strait, while the European Union's naval force Aspides warned that ships linked to Israel, the United States, or Saudi Arabia face heightened attack risk and should avoid the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden entirely.

Tanker Diversions Signal Real Supply Impact

The threats have already translated into commercial disruption. Two oil tankers carrying Saudi crude to Asia reversed course in the Red Sea on Tuesday, with shipping data on LSEG showing them heading toward the Suez Canal instead. Asian refiners are now seeking to ship Saudi crude from the Red Sea port of Yanbu through the Suez and around Africa — a significantly longer and costlier route.

"The energy market now has the dual-strait worry, with the Bab el-Mandeb Strait looking like it could join the Strait of Hormuz as a hot spot."

— Tim Waterer, Chief Market Analyst, KCM Trade

The market structure reflects the supply anxiety. The Brent three-month timespread expanded to $9.26 a barrel — its widest since May 22 — deepening the backwardation that signals traders expect near-term supply to remain tight relative to future months.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking in Manila, said Iran was "not serious about talks," while adding that the US remained "always committed to diplomacy." The comment dampened hopes for a near-term de-escalation.

India Faces Mounting Energy Import Pressure

For India, the world's third-largest oil importer, the price trajectory carries significant macroeconomic consequences. Brent crude has risen nearly a third since the start of July, when it was trading around $71. Every $10-per-barrel increase in oil prices widens India's current account deficit by approximately 0.4% of GDP and adds pressure on the rupee, which has already weakened as import costs mount.

Indian refiners — the largest buyers of Saudi crude after China — face particular exposure to the shipping disruptions. The longer routes around Africa add transit time and freight costs, while higher insurance premiums for Red Sea and Gulf passages compound the expense.

Fundamental Disconnect Persists

Despite the price surge, analysts caution that the underlying market remains oversupplied. US crude inventories rose by 2 million barrels to 411.7 million barrels in the week ended July 17, the Energy Information Administration reported Wednesday — exceeding analysts' expectations for a 1.1 million-barrel draw. OPEC+ continues to signal production discipline, but the group's spare capacity means any de-escalation could rapidly deflate the geopolitical premium.

The result is a sharply asymmetric setup: a violent upside tail toward $117-plus on a Hormuz disruption, against a substantial downside pull toward the low $70s if diplomacy succeeds. For now, the war premium is in control — and the market is watching two straits, not one.
